Compositional Phenotype Representations and Clinical Prior Distillation

for Missense Variant-Disease Association Retrieval

Abstract

Missense variants are by far the most prevalent type of pathogenic coding variants, but

they are predominantly annotated as variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in ClinVar.

This categorization prevents any medical intervention despite the variant being causal. Ex-

isting computational tools predict pathogenicity well but cannot answer the question that

drives genetic diagnosis: harmful for which disease? We present PheMART2, a contrastive

retrieval framework that ranks candidate diseases for each query missense variant. To

solve these problems, we implement two major architectural designs to improve general-

ization. Diseases are encoded using weighted attention-based combinations of HPO terms

instead of relying on concept IDs, allowing the model to generalize to disease labels outside

the training distribution. Population-scale variant–phenotype relationships from the MVP

phenome-wide association study are mapped to the HPO disease space through a curated

CUI mapping and SapBERT-based semantic translation pipeline, and then distilled into

our model using bidirectional Kullback-Leibler divergence in both the variant→disease and

disease→variant directions. Model evaluation is performed by randomly splitting data on

the basis of genes instead of per-variant random splits with negative sampling, across all

1,563 diseases in the dataset. In comparison with this more stringent evaluation approach,

PheMART2 demonstrates an MRR of 0.272 for unseen genes, an 18.1% improvement over

the no-KL, no-auxiliary version (p = 0.001), with the clinical prior distillation being the

## Chapter 1: Introduction

### 1.1 Background

The average person carries about 9,000 missense mutations compared to the reference human

genome. Only a small fraction of these missense variants is medically actionable, while the

rest is either benign or, much more often, uninterpretable. Today, more than 70% of all

missense variants listed in ClinVar belong to the group of variants of uncertain significance

(VUS) (Landrum et al., 2020), meaning that clinicians can use them to guide clinical decision

making despite clear underlying causality. Loss of function mutations, like nonsense and

frameshift alleles, interfere with protein functionality directly; by comparison, missense

mutations are not always detrimental to protein structure. An amino acid change may

be harmless in certain positions but harmful in other contexts, depending on side chain

properties, structural environment, and domain specificity.

There are two features of the missense variant analysis problem that complicate inference.

First, the very same substitution in the protein sequence might be responsible for an actual

disease manifestation in one condition but irrelevant in another; additionally, there might

be disease-specific predictions for various functional regions in a single gene, as in the case of

MFN2, where variants in different functional regions contribute to different Charcot-Marie-

Tooth types. The second characteristic of the missense variant inference problem is a lack

of training data; typically, fewer than ten annotated missense variants are known to cause

a given disease listed in ClinVar.

Predictive computational approaches to missense variant analysis have been improving

steadily in recent years, with methods like AlphaMissense, CADD, REVEL, EVE, and

more recent protein language models used for identifying whether a mutation is harmful

(“likely pathogenic”) or not. This question is clearly defined and, at this point, is easy to

solve using machine learning techniques. However, this approach solves only half of the

equation, as clinicians are interested in addressing the second question: harmful for which

disease? A classification of a mutation as “likely pathogenic” is useless from the standpoint

of medical diagnosis, since the mutation could be causing any number of conditions, from

metabolic syndrome to neurological and structural heart conditions.

This thesis aims to answer the second question, namely, to rank disease candidates, defined

as a collection of Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms, in order of predicted likelihood

of association with a particular missense mutation. Although ClinVar provides training

examples exclusively for rare Mendelian diseases, the proposed formulation does not confine

its application to the field of rare diseases alone.

### 1.2 Related Work

1.2.1 Pathogenicity Prediction

The existing methods for estimating the effect of missense variants can be classified into

four broad groups. Scores based on conservation—SIFT (Vaser et al., 2016), PhyloP, phast-

Cons, GERP++—operate under the assumption that functionally important sites will be

conserved among different species. Ensembles combine many features using machine learn-

ing: CADD (Rentzsch et al., 2019) combines over 60 features through logistic regression on

simulated de novo mutations; REVEL (Ioannidis et al., 2016) uses random forests on top

of 13 predictors; and recent models (ClinPred, BayesDel, MetaRNN) use neural networks

revolutionized the field. ESM-1b (Rives et al., 2021), trained on 250 million proteins using

masked language modelling, represents the evolution constraints without performing any

alignment; recently, it was shown that its zero-shot log-likelihood ratio allows classifying

pathogenicity genome-wide (Brandes et al., 2023). ESM-2 (Lin et al., 2023) extends the

approach up to 15 billion parameters and adds atomic-resolution structure modelling capa-

of the evolutionary sequences, classifying variants without training labels and covering over

36 million variants on 3,219 disease genes. Methods based on protein structures are another

group. AlphaMissense (Cheng et al., 2023) extends the AlphaFold framework along with

a primate frequency database in order to annotate 89% of all human missense variants;

gMVP (H. Zhang et al., 2022) uses a graph attention network with coevolutionary edges;

and PreMode (Zhong et al., 2025) employs a SE(3)-equivariant graph network to classify

gain vs. loss-of-function missense variants.

These methods show impressive accuracy, and several have already become standard compo-

nents of clinical variant interpretation pipelines. None of them, however, takes into account

a specific target disease.

1.2.2 Disease-Conditioned Variant Interpretation

A smaller body of work has begun to address variant–disease specificity. V2P (Stein et al.,

2025) extends variant effect prediction to 23 HPO phenotype categories, learning category-

specific pathogenicity thresholds and showing that variant effects are indeed phenotype-

dependent. The granularity is coarse — a category such as ‘abnormality of the nervous

system’ subsumes thousands of distinct diseases — and patient-level interpretation requires

1.2.3 Knowledge Distillation and Population-Level Clinical Data

Knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from a teacher model to a student by aligning

their output distributions. The technique was originally a model compression tool; in

biomedical natural language processing it has been used to compress large language models

for clinical text mining with little loss in performance (Gu et al., 2023). Its application to

genomic variant interpretation, in contrast, remains essentially unexplored.

Cross-ontology mapping is the prerequisite for using population-level clinical data in this

setting. The biomedical domain hosts multiple ontologies that describe overlapping clinical

concepts from different angles: ICD-10 for hospital billing, LOINC for lab tests, PheCodes

for ICD aggregations, and HPO for individual phenotypic features. The mapping between

these vocabularies is sparse — only 2.2% of ICD codes have a direct HPO mapping. Prior

work has bridged the HPO–PheCode gap with curated mappings, and SapBERT (F. Liu

et al., 2021) provides a biomedical entity-linking model whose embedding similarities yield

approximate mappings between heterogeneous concept vocabularies.

Phenome-wide association studies at population scale produce large numbers of variant–

phenotype associations across thousands of clinical concepts, but no prior work has used

these associations as a teacher signal for variant-disease prediction. The bidirectional VD-

KL distillation in this thesis fills that gap, using a curated CUI mapping for direct ontological

1.2.4 Heterogeneous Graphs in Genomics

Biological knowledge contains an innate graph structure. Protein-protein interactions de-

scribe relationships between genes, while Human Phenotype Ontology encodes hierarchy

and semantics between phenotypes. The heterogeneous graph transformer (HGT) (Hu et

al., 2020) generalizes graph attention to multiple node and edge types and has been success-

ful on web-scale relational graphs. In genomics, most graph neural network applications

function at the gene level – e.g., gene function prediction in PPI networks, disease-gene asso-

ciation prediction over integrated biological networks, and phenotype propagation in HPO.

Variant-level graph reasoning has not been extensively explored. Here, HGT is applied to

propagate information along a heterogeneous gene-trait graph, allowing variant-level pre-

dictions to benefit from network neighbors even if the immediate gene context is sparsely

annotated.

1.2.5 Phenotype-Driven Diagnostic Tools

Diagnosis of rare diseases has become increasingly computational. Exomiser (Robinson et

al., 2014) is currently the most widely used phenotype-driven variant prioritizer, integrating

variant filtering with cross-species phenotype comparison; recently proposed processing im-

provements have increased top-10 accuracy on genome sequencing data from 49.7% to 85.5%

(Cooperstein et al., 2025). LIRICAL (Robinson et al., 2020) uses likelihood-ratio scoring

with interpretable per-disease evidence and places the correct diagnosis first in 24.5% of

cases. Recent comparative analyses show complementary strengths between Exomiser and

LIRICAL, implying their combined usage with largely uncorrelated rankings. Other tools

Recent advancements in the field include large language models (LLMs) in this task domain.

DeepRare (W. Zhao et al., 2026) incorporates more than 40 specialized tools in an agentic

them by providing variant-disease embeddings that allow ranking through retrieval-based

search over all candidate diseases at once, functioning as a retrieval module in an agentic

diagnostic pipeline.

1.2.6 Electronic Health Records (EHR) and PheWAS Data

Electronic health records contain phenotypic data increasingly used in genomic research.

Phenome-wide association studies (PheWAS) compare genetic variants to all EHR-derived

phenotypes for a cohort, elucidating pleiotropy of common variants and identifying novel

gene-phenotype associations. The Million Veteran Program (MVP) (Verma et al., 2024) is

the largest multi-ancestry PheWAS dataset to date, including 2,068 phenotypes in 635,969

subjects. The UK Biobank (Bycroft et al., 2018) is an additional resource for deep pheno-

typing and genomic data on about half a million individuals. EHR-based phenotyping has

1.3 Approach and Contributions

Three open problems remain in the field. Firstly, generalization to disease labels not seen in

training: current disease-conditioned models rely on a fixed disease vocabulary (V2P) or re-

quire per-disease fine-tuning (DYNA), and gene-level approaches (Exomiser, SHEPHERD)

cannot generalize to the variant level. Secondly, population-level clinical data integration:

PheWAS resources like MVP encode abundant variant-phenotype associations over thou-

sands of concepts, but their concept space (ICD-10/LOINC/PheCode) is incompatible with

the HPO-based disease space used in genetic diagnoses. Thirdly, label eﬀiciency: there are

only a few annotated pathogenic variants per disease in ClinVar.

PheMART2 addresses these aspects in a unified retrieval framework. Diseases are encoded

using attention-weighted composition of HPO terms, allowing inference time queries by

providing the corresponding HPO terms without training. MVP PheWAS associations are

mapped to HPO disease space using a curated UMLS Concept Unique Identifier (CUI)

mapping to achieve direct ontology mappings, and via a SapBERT-based semantic bridging

method for remaining associations. These are distilled into the model using bidirectional KL

divergence in both the variant->disease and disease->variant directions. Distillation serves

as supervision for variants with sparse ClinVar labels; Section 3.4 demonstrates that the

effect increases as the proportion of labeled variants shrinks – at 5% of the training labels,

## Chapter 2: Methods

AI-tool use in this chapter: prose clarity refinement (Claude, ChatGPT) and code assistance for data

preprocessing, training pipeline, and evaluation scripts (Claude Code, Codex). All architectural

choices, training-objective design, and evaluation-protocol decisions are the author’s.

2.1 Problem Formulation

The prediction of association between variants and diseases is modeled as a retrieval task,

where each disease is associated with one or more HPO phenotype terms and binary label

values are obtained from pathogenic and likely pathogenic variant annotations in ClinVar. In

inference time, the variant of interest is compared to all diseases in the set of candidates and

ranks are obtained. The effectiveness of the retrieval model is assessed by measuring MRR

with respect to 1,563 candidate diseases. The method used differs from that introduced in

the previous section, as the prediction model generates ranks rather than binary scores.

2.2 Data Sources and Preprocessing

2.2.1 Main Task: Variant-Disease Associations

The disease-variant mappings are taken from ClinVar (Landrum et al., 2020). The data set

at hand includes 53,237 mappings associated with 42,452 unique missense variants, 3,217

genes, and 1,563 diseases. After filtering for those mappings for which we have both ESM-2

and protein sequence embeddings, there are 46,327 mappings representing about 32,000

variants. Every mapping has an HGVS naming convention, a linked gene, and a disease

identifier. The descriptions of diseases are compositional since each of 1,563 diseases consists

2.2.2 Variant and Protein Features

The features of the variants come from ESM-2 (Lin et al., 2023), a language model for

proteins that has 15 billion parameters. The DeltaP embeddings, which correspond to

the difference between the ESM-2 embeddings of the mutant and wild-type versions of the

variant at the specific position, are used to construct 1280-dimensional vectors for each

variant. The protein sequence features consist of mean-pooled ESM-2 embeddings for the

whole reference sequence. The 1280-dimensional vector is constructed for each gene. We

use RefSeq sequences from NCBI because ClinVar annotations are made based on RefSeq

accessions.

2.2.3 Heterogeneous Knowledge Graph

Our knowledge graph contains two kinds of nodes – genes and HPO traits, and three different

edge types. Genes interact with other genes according to the protein-protein interactions

from STRING (Szklarczyk et al., 2021), which are represented with 768-dimensional gene

embeddings. Gene-trait edges are formed based on known associations between genes and

phenotypes from HPO (Köhler et al., 2021). The trait-trait interaction consists of the HPO

is_a hierarchy and k-nearest neighbors based on the 768-dimensional HPO term embeddings.

Gene embeddings are created using SapBERT (F. Liu et al., 2021) embeddings of their

descriptions. All node embeddings are projected to a common hidden dimension of 256 in

the HGT encoder.

The graph is undirected (edges duplicated), and it is kept the same for train, validation,

and test split of the dataset. Such a configuration represents the transductive version of

GNN, where we only partition the variant-disease labels, while the biological graph with

2.2.5 Clinical Prior Teacher: MVP PheWAS

The teacher signal is built from the Million Veteran Program (MVP) PheWAS study (Verma

et al., 2024), a phenome-wide association study covering 635,969 participants across four

ancestry groups (European, African, Admixed American, East Asian). We use MVP as a

sparse variant-phenotype co-occurrence matrix containing 142,055 rsIDs and 17,086 clinical

concepts drawn from UMLS CUI (38.9%), LOINC (34.5%), PheCodes (10.8%), RXNORM

(9.2%) and ICD-10 (2.8%) code ontologies; the matrix was assembled in collaboration with

the MVP study group from the per-ancestry summary statistics. We restrict the teacher to

the European-ancestry matrix and retain 5,425 concepts after L1-norm filtering on concept

quality.

The MVP concept ontology (ICD-10/LOINC/PheCode) is not consistent with the HPO dis-

ease ontology. As such, MVP concepts are mapped to diseases through two complementary

methods. First, CUI-based mapping was manually curated from UMLS Concept Unique

Identifiers to the disease index set, and includes 459 out of 1,563 diseases. Second, semantic

bridging is performed between the HPO and MVP ontologies using SapBERT; the closest k

hits with at least similarity score of 0.35 for each HPO term are included, resulting in com-

plete coverage of all 1,563 diseases. Combining the two methods yields a sparse distribution

of teachers for each MVP disease across diseases (the full mapping pipeline is summarised

as a Sankey diagram in Figure S1). It should be noted that only 10.8% of training variants

(2,860 of 26,404) in the gene-holdout split have MVP coverage.

Different mapping strategies trade off coverage and precision: CUI-based curation is high-

precision but low-coverage, whereas SapBERT semantic bridging gives full coverage at the

cost of weaker per-edge confidence. The choice of mapping is therefore itself a hyperparam-

2.2.6 Data Splitting

Three different data splits are considered. Gene-holdout (primary) splits by gene with

70/15/15 ratio for training/validation/testing. Gene sizes are stratified and the split is

done in such a way that no gene appears in both training and testing sets. Disease-holdout

holds out all diseases – diseases in the test split have zero labels in the training set. This

split aims to evaluate out-of-distribution disease inference, with all HPO traits belonging

to these diseases being included in the graph (transductive). Within-gene splits by variant

within the same gene – this is done exclusively for sanity checks, since there is known

information leakage due to the correlations between variants.

2.3 Model Architecture

The model consists of four components, illustrated in Figure 2.1: the variant and protein

encoders using features of ESM-2 model, the graph encoder working with the heterogeneous

gene-trait graph, the disease encoder processing HPO-based disease representations, and the

multimodal fusion module aggregating the variant, protein, and gene representations.

2.3.1 Variant and Protein Encoders

The variant and the protein-sequence encoders are two-layer MLPs with LayerNorm and

ReLU activation functions mapping 1280-dimensional ESM-2 features to a unified 128-

dimensional representation. The variant encoder processes DeltaP embeddings to produce

per-variant representation. The protein encoder processes gene-level mean-pooling of se-

quence embeddings to provide a gene-level protein embedding. This gene-level protein

embedding is indexable at the variant level, so the protein representation of all variants

from the same gene is identical.

2.3.2 Graph Encoder

The graph encoder is realized as a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT) (Hu et al.,

2020). Type-specific projections increase dimensions of gene and trait features and transfer

them to a common hidden space, followed by two-layer HGTConv aggregation with residual

connections and dropout of two heads of attention per each of three possible edges. The

type-specific projections provide the final node embeddings. The graph encoder works with

the entire graph on each training step (it contains less than 30,000 nodes) and uses a

separate learning-rate controlled parameter group to facilitate converging of the graph with

the rest of the training process. The NoGraphEncoder control variant replaces HGTConv

operations with an MLP with equal capacity but no message passing between nodes.

2.3.3 Disease Encoder

The disease encoder produces a disease embedding from an HPO trait set. At the first

step, the HGT outputs of all traits are retrieved, then processed with a shared MLP. Next,

pooling occurs with scaled dot product attention. While training, trait dropout is applied

with probability 0.15 per term (ensuring presence of at least one trait per set). The encoder

also receives the additive log-cardinality bias to get access to HPO trait set size. Since

each disease is defined by the HPO term set, not the embedding, an unseen disease can be

queried during inference just by providing its set of HPO terms. As a control, Disease-ID

baseline variant uses a learned embedding table to produce a disease embedding instead of

attention pooling, so it cannot produce embeddings for unseen diseases.

2.3.4 Multimodal Fusion

The fusion module aggregates variant, protein, and gene-level graph embeddings associated

with the variant in question through a residual gate. The fusion MLP maps concatenated

modality embeddings to the unified hidden representation with residual connections and

gate. It uses LayerNorm, ReLU, Dropout, and learned residual gate (which is clamped

at 0.4). During training, modality dropout is applied with probability 0.05 (variants), 0.3

(protein), and 0.3 (gene). It is guaranteed that the variant modality would be available if

all three modalities are dropped.

2.4 Training Objectives

2.4.1 Contrastive Retrieval Loss

The main loss function is contrastive loss in the vein of CLIP (Radford et al., 2021). Vari-

ant and disease embeddings are separately passed through two-layer MLPs and normalized

L2, and their similarity is rescaled with learnable logit temperature that’s clipped by a

configurable maximum. Given that each ClinVar variant may be labeled with several differ-

ent diseases, the contrastive loss is applied multi-positive softmax style against the whole

disease dictionary, with the denominator covering all 1,563 diseases. Per-example weights

de-emphasize highly common diseases using an inverse square-root frequency weighting. La-

bel smoothing is implemented as a convex mixture with uniform distribution, serving as

the control.

2.4.2 Auxiliary Tasks

Domain prediction consists of a sampled InfoNCE loss between variant embeddings and pro-

totype embeddings of 769 Pfam domains, using 63 randomly sampled negative prototypes

per variant.

Functional impact prediction consists of four heads sharing the same encoder architecture:

three regression heads (Conservation, Protein Impact, Integrative) using masked Smooth

L1 loss, and one mechanism classification head using masked binary cross-entropy against

nine classes (positive class weight 3.0 to address the problem of class imbalance); losses for

all four heads are aggregated with a weighted sum, where axis-wise weights add up to one.

2.4.3 VD-KL Clinical Prior Distillation

The clinical prior MVP teacher is distilled into the student using bi-directional KL diver-

gence loss. In the variant-to-disease direction, the KL loss attempts to match the student’s

predicted distribution over diseases to the projection of the teacher’s distribution onto dis-

eases, with only variants whose total teacher-mapped mass exceeds 0.05 participating in

the KL loss so that the teacher acts on well-grounded concepts and doesn’t corrupt high

confidence predictions. In the disease-to-variant direction, the student is trained on a candi-

date variant set per disease comprising up to 8 positive variants, up to 32 priority variants

suggested by the teacher, and 128 random negative variants. The KL loss matches the

student’s predicted distribution over this candidate set to the teacher’s distribution.

VD-KL loss scheduling follows a warm-up strategy. For the first three epochs, only the main

contrastive task runs in order to give the encoder reasonable initialization. Afterwards, the

KL loss weight is increased linearly until epoch 3 + 8 with its final value being 0.6; starting

from epoch 3 + 5, the disease-to-variant direction of the loss becomes active. Final weights

of the KL loss favor the variant-to-disease direction more than the other one. The max logit

temperature used by the main contrastive task is lowered to avoid sharpness in the softmax

distribution of the student model, because a peaky main-task distribution would both reduce

the KL loss and raise the KL loss by increasing KL weight dynamically. Adaptive weight

scaling is not enabled for this reason, since the max logit temperature and KL loss create a

positive feedback loop.

2.4.4 Total Loss and Optimization

The five loss functions—contrastive loss, domain loss, functional impact loss, KL loss from

variant to disease, and KL loss from disease to variant—are combined according to their

weights. For optimization, the AdamW optimizer with weight decay and gradient clipping

at an L2 norm of 5.0 is used, and a separate parameter group is assigned to the graph

encoder. The learning rate scheduler uses cosine annealing with warm restarts (𝑇0 = 20,

𝑇mult = 2). Batch size is set to 128, while domain predictions are made every other epoch

and functional impact predictions every epoch. Early stopping is performed based on gene-

macro nDCG@10, with patience set to 20.

2.5 Evaluation Metrics

2.5.1 Retrieval Metrics

For each test variant, all 1,563 diseases are scored, and the following metrics are computed:

primarily MRR (mean reciprocal rank) over test variants under tie-aware expected ranks;

nDCG@10 with binary relevance; Recall@k for multiple k values under tie-aware expected

probability; the Median Rank of the best positive disease; and AUROC/AUPRC, consider-

ing each test query as a per-variant binary classification problem.

2.5.2 Stratified Analysis

Two stratifications are applied to all results tables: (i) Training-support buckets classify

test variant-disease pairs into low, medium, and high support according to the frequency

of diseases in the training set. Note that this stratification is an indicator of annotation

support during training rather than disease prevalence, since a rare clinical condition can

appear in the “high” bucket if it is suﬀiciently well-studied genetically. (ii) Disease system

categories associate each disease with one of the 12 HPO biological systems (e.g., neurologi-

cal, musculoskeletal, cardiovascular) using HPO hierarchy, allowing for stratified evaluation

of model performance across organs/systems.

In addition to regular averaging, gene-macro averages (metrics averaged on a per-gene basis

instead of per pair) are also reported to avoid overweighting of metrics associated with genes

having many test variants. The early-stopping criterion is set to gene-macro nDCG@10.

2.5.3 Statistical Testing

Experiments are run five times with independent random seeds; for a small subset of

compute-heavy ablation studies, three seeds are used. Cross-configuration statistical test-

3.6 Comparison with PheMART v1 Model

PheMART v1 [Wen et al. (2026)] is the prior generation of the PheMART model line.

It performs contrastive learning between missense variants and HPO-composed phenotype

targets, using a TensorFlow variational autoencoder on the variant side and CODER+EHR

phenotype embeddings on the concept side. Its published headline performance is auROC

= 0.972, measured under per-variant 10-fold cross-validation in which each variant is ranked

against 31 sampled negatives. In this per-variant random split setup, it is possible to include

some variants with the same genes in both train and test data splits, meaning that many test

variants have common genes with training variants, allowing the model to take advantage of

those close relations when making correct predictions. However, the problem that arises in

clinical genetic diagnosis is related to the ability to generalize across unseen genes. For this

task, the per-variant random CV protocol is not relevant; hence, a gene-holdout strategy is

necessary.

To enable a head-to-head comparison under the clinically relevant protocol, we ran a

matched gene-holdout evaluation. We re-trained and re-evaluated PheMART v1 under

a strict gene-holdout split — no genes shared between training and test sets, matching

the construction of our gene-holdout v5 protocol — and obtained auROC = 0.721. The

retraining strictly followed the original v1 protocol, training data, and architecture, so that

v1’s published methodology is preserved as the comparison reference. PheMART2 M4 was

evaluated on the gene-holdout v5 test split across all 1,563 candidate diseases and reached

auROC = 0.885 (Table 4). The generational improvement on unseen genes is therefore

+0.16 absolute auROC, or +23% relative. The 0.25 auROC drop on v1 between its native

## Chapter 5: Discussion

5.1 Summary of Findings

PheMART2 is introduced in this dissertation as a framework for retrieval of associations

between missense variants and diseases, which incorporates features such as ESM2 protein

language model, heterogeneous graph message passing, compositional HPO disease repre-

sentations, and population-level clinical prior distillation. The major findings are as follows:

First, the full model (M4) achieves 18.1% MRR increase on held-out genes that are not

seen in training supervision but appear in the biological knowledge graph (0.272 vs 0.230,

p = 0.001). In this transductive learning setup, held-out genes still retain the same PPI

and HPO annotation. The reason why it can be seen as the clinically most relevant setting

is that the majority of candidate genes observed in clinical sequencing already have some

level of biological annotation. KL distillation turns out to be the main contributor in

terms of performance gain (+14.4%, p = 0.039), while the auxiliary tasks only help through

interaction. HPO compositional representation of disease is crucial for out-of-distribution

inference without further training data; disease holdout MRR is 0.39 for all configurations,

significantly exceeding gene holdout MRR (0.23 - 0.27). Compositional HPO representation

is better than fixed representations of diseases by 21% in AUROC.

Second, the clinical prior distillation performs best where the data is scarce: the 5% data

MRR gain is 38.3%. Furthermore, the MRR increase holds for any data availability regime,

achieving its maximum values where there is the least amount of data. On external datasets

the model shows robust generalization on task-aligned data (676 points from Phenopackets

dataset with 0% variant overlap, MRR = 0.291). For those genes observed during training

the MRR equals 0.418, while for unseen MRR is only 0.089. The model retrieves the correct

disease in the top-10 list 51.5% of the time.

Lastly, HGT graph encoder and KL distillation work positively with one another. Without

KL distillation, HGT does not make any improvements and may even decrease the score

(-4.0%, no significance). In combination with KL distillation, HGT increases the KL signal

(+4.4%). It suggests that the graph geometry helps the model to better exploit the clinical

prior distribution.

5.2 Relation to Prior Work

5.2.1 Disease-Specific Variant Interpretation

It was mentioned in the introduction that current disease-conditioned methods for variant

interpretation perform their task at different levels of granularity and there is no benchmark

comparing them side-by-side. The internal ablation scheme applied in this thesis (M1-M4,

Disease-ID ablation, shuffled teacher, label smoothing) allows one to estimate the impact of

individual components on the final result, but does not say whether or not PheMART2 is

better compared to other approaches for similar tasks. The closest generation-to-generation

comparison available is the matched gene-holdout evaluation against PheMART v1 (Wen et

al., 2026), which yields an absolute AUROC gain of +0.16 attributable to the architectural

and training-objective changes introduced in PheMART2.

One unique property of PheMART2 in the context of comparison is the problem formulation

itself: instead of producing a classification for 1,563 diseases, the system ranks them. This

opens a possibility of open-world problem statement, where new disease definitions can be

retrieved without retraining. It is worth mentioning that disease holdout generalization is

only possible due to this property. It would be a useful direction of future research to set a

standardized benchmark for variant-disease retrieval.

5.2.2 Clinical Prior Utilization

As far as we know, this work is the first to use population-level PheWAS association signal

for clinical prior as a teacher signal. The MVP dataset (Verma et al., 2024) has a rich

history of being used as a fertile ground for obtaining cross-disease associations and has

been widely applied in GWAS settings before.

Cross-ontology mapping, i.e., mapping of heterogeneous MVP concepts (ICD-10, LOINC,

PheCode, RXNORM) to the HPO-defined disease space, was performed using two strategies:

direct CUI mapping for identical concepts and SapBERT-based semantic linking. We needed

such a combination because of fragmentation in biomedical knowledge systems: only 2.2%

of ICD-10 codes directly link to HPO (X. A. Zhang et al., 2024).

Despite the low teacher signal coverage (only 10.8% of training variants), it consistently

improves performance on the aggregate metric, indicating dense information in a partial

prior. However, the effect is inconsistent: bucket-level analysis shows that KL distillation

mostly helps for variants associated with well-annotated diseases (+14.8% MRR improve-

ment in the frequent bucket) and has either no impact or is detrimental to the performance

of variants associated with rare diseases (approximately -12.4% MRR improvement in the

rare bucket). Such a pattern reflects bias towards well-studied genes with extensive clinical

annotation in the MVP dataset. Therefore, the clinical prior should be considered as a

high-support prior improving retrieval quality for diseases with extensive ClinVar annota-

tion (and where the MVP teacher signal also covers the disease better), rather than as a

48


<!-- Page 61 -->


Chapter 5. Discussion

universal prior that provides an advantage to all diseases. Importantly, high support means

high support in ClinVar annotation, rather than clinical disease prevalence—clinically rare

disease can still have high support in ClinVar due to genetic studies of this condition. The

mapped variants help to establish a bridge from a limited space covered by this teacher to

wider parts of the variant space through representations. This bridge is most helpful for

diseases that have some EHR representation.

Still, there is one drawback to consider regarding the clinical prior. Population-level clinical

priors are influenced by prevalence of particular diseases in the source cohort, thus may fail

to catch clinically significant associations. For instance, the distribution of ICD-10 codes

naturally favors orthopedic problems in MVP patients over cancers. Bias towards such

well-populated diseases in our teacher signal becomes a limitation of the current clinical

prior, which cannot be fixed by improving the mapping and requires re-weighting of the

signal itself.

5.2.3 Phenotype-Driven Diagnosis Tools

Our approach differs in the problem domain from similar clinical tools, such as Exomiser

(Robinson et al., 2014) and LIRICAL (Robinson et al., 2020), as it takes a variant-level

approach, using a likelihood ratio method to make decisions.

Recently obtained successes in using large language models (LLMs) for developing diag-

nostic assistants (W. Zhao et al., 2026) reignited discussions on whether embedding-based

approaches are still useful. While LLMs perform excellently in incorporating free text clin-

ical narratives into a model, they lack the ability to work in the continuous representation

space for systematic search across hundreds of diseases. Our embeddings can be readily

incorporated as the retrieval module in an LLM-based diagnosis tool.

### 5.3 Limitations

A few limitations must be recognized while considering the presented results. First, the

signal extracted for the teacher from the MVP data is inherently limited and biased because

only 10.8% of the variants are included, with the vast majority of these variants pertaining

to well-known genes. This corresponds to the fact that gains based on KL-divergence

are higher in high-support regions and lower in low-support regions, rather than being

opposite to the expectation that additional supervision would aid underrepresented variants.

The second limitation stems directly from the transductive nature of the model in use:

evaluation of novel genes on phenopackets demonstrates large performance drop (MRR =

0.418 for training-graph genes vs 0.089 for novel genes). In particular, this happens since

the model is heavily dependent on neighborhood-based features, which cannot be defined

for genes that were not seen before. The third limitation concerns the type of mutations

considered by this framework, which is currently limited to missense mutations, as only

ESM-2 DeltaP embedding can handle such mutations. In order to account for other types of

mutations, such as nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, or regulatory, new embedding schemes

need to be developed. Other potential limitations include bias of the ClinVar database

towards well-studied genes and curation issues. The former limitation is confirmed by the

baseline with only HPO information (MRR = 0.030), which indicates no utilization of

obvious HPO associations. However, the dataset bias is still present. In addition, power

of several experiments is limited because ablations based on multiple random seeds are

computationally expensive; hence, several ablations are conducted using three seeds, leading

to larger confidence intervals and uncertainty around estimates. Finally, teacher signal based

on MVP is time-limited because MVP data are available up to 2020, while the ClinVar

database grew considerably after that date.

5.4 Future Directions

There are three clear extensions following from the above limitations.

Broadening clinical priors. Limitations related to teacher coverage and temporal aspect lead

to broadening clinical priors. Integration of PheWAS data from sources such as UK Biobank

(Bycroft et al., 2018), All of Us, and BioBank Japan increases diversity of the population

base, while re-estimating the MVP co-occurrence matrix using more recent EHR snapshots

will take care of the temporal limitation. Improved cross-ontology mapping (using either

biomedical language models such as BERT, or the Mondo ontology) can boost the strength

of the bridge between MVP concepts and diseases defined with HPO.

Graph-based extension for novel genes. Limitations regarding the novel genes call for an

architecture able to handle new gene nodes at inference time, relying solely on the connec-

tivity provided by PPI neighborhoods and HPO annotations. Together with multi-modal

variant features (for example, language models on DNA sequences to cover splice and regula-

tory variants, protein truncation feature for nonsense variants), it would enable a clinically

useful model going beyond the missense variants.

External validation and clinical integration. Validation on external datasets such as Undi-

agnosed Diseases Network (UDN), 100,000 Genomes Project, and DECIPHER would help

determine if the gains made on Phenopackets apply to undiagnosed patients, once data are

made available. In addition to validation, the model itself should be thought of as a module

for retrieving disease annotations from variants. Integration with patient-level HPO phe-

notype information (by restricting the possible disease set or reweighting embeddings by

HPO similarities), followed by integration into the existing pipelines such as Exomiser and

LIRICAL would enable the translation into clinical practice.

## Chapter 6: Conclusion

Prediction of disease association of missense variants remains diﬀicult in the translation

of genomic sequencing to medical diagnosis. Current methods are either disease-agnostic

or cannot generalize outside their training data. In this thesis, we propose PheMART2, a

retrieval-based framework for predicting missense variant-disease associations based on two

major innovations: compositional disease representations using Human Phenotype Ontology

(HPO) terms, and bidirectional knowledge distillation (KL distillation) of population-level

MVP PheWAS clinical priors.

We validate that our compositional disease representation design choice is well-founded.

Our model obtains a MRR score of 0.39 in predicting missense variant-disease associations

from out-of-distribution disease labels, without any external training signals, and the repre-

sentation enables such generalization as it is an intrinsic characteristic that does not require

knowledge distillation or auxiliary learning objectives.

With respect to knowledge distillation, our clinical prior distillation improves missense

variant-disease retrieval by 14.4% (p = 0.039) in predicting novel biologically annotated

genes held out during model training. Our improvements have been confirmed to be driven

by valid clinical prior information through the use of shuffled-teacher and label smoothing

controls. We find that the teacher plays its most important role in helping the student learn

when there is little training data available (38.3% improvement at 5% data).

In an evaluation on an independently curated cohort of 676 Phenopackets cases with no
